chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Profit and Loss Statement

lessons.title: Reading a Profit and Loss Statement Line by Line: From Revenue to Net Profit

children.text: The profit and loss statement is a waterfall. Revenue goes in at the top, and every line below it is somebody taking a cut: suppliers, employees, landlords, lenders, the tax department. Whatever survives to the bottom belongs to the shareholders.

Managers who can read this waterfall ask better questions. Instead of "why is profit down?", they ask "our revenue grew 7% but material cost grew 11%, what happened to input prices?" This lesson walks the waterfall line by line, in the exact order Indian companies present it.

body.text: Never read the P&L as a single profit number. Read it as a sequence of subtractions, and find the line where your company loses more than it should.

children.text: The Order Is Fixed by Law

Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format of the statement of profit and loss, so the sequence below is the same at every Indian company. Here is Kesari Foods, the fictional Indore snacks company from Lesson 1.1, in full Schedule III shape.

body.caption: Kesari Foods: statement of profit and loss for FY25 (₹ crore)

cells: Sales of snacks, the core business, net of GST and discounts
Interest on deposits, rent from a spare godown, gains on sale of assets
Flour, oil, spices, packaging actually used in production
Negative because closing stock is higher than opening stock
Salaries, bonus, provident fund, gratuity, staff welfare
Interest on term loans and the cash credit line
This year's share of the cost of machines, vehicles and software
Rent, power, freight, advertising, travel, audit fees and the rest

body.text: The "changes in inventories" line confuses almost everyone. It is not a cost. It is a correction. Cost of materials counts everything bought and consumed, but some of that production is still sitting in the warehouse unsold. A negative figure means stock went up, so costs are reduced this year and will be charged when the stock is sold.

body.title: Build the bottom line
body.prompt: Using the Kesari Foods figures above, if the tax expense had been ₹1.5 crore instead of ₹1.3 crore, what would profit for the year be, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Profit before tax stays at ₹5.0 crore, because tax is charged after it. ₹5.0 crore minus ₹1.5 crore = ₹3.5 crore. Tax changes the bottom line without touching operating performance, which is why analysts look at profit before tax when comparing years.

children.text: Line by Line, From the Top
Each line has a trap in it. These are the ones managers fall into.
Revenue from operations

is what the company earns from its main business. It is reported net of GST, because GST is collected on the government's behalf and was never the company's money. It is also net of trade discounts and expected returns. Bill ₹118 including 18% GST and the P&L shows ₹100.
Other income

is everything outside the core business: interest on fixed deposits, dividends, rent, foreign exchange gains, profit on selling an old asset. It is real money, but it is not performance. A company whose profit grew only because of treasury income has not had a good year.
Cost of materials consumed

is what a manufacturer used up in production. A trading business shows purchases of stock-in-trade instead. A services business often shows neither, which is why a P&L looks so different across industries.
Employee benefits expense
covers far more than salaries: bonus, provident fund and gratuity, share-based payments and staff welfare. In a services company this is the largest line on the page.
Finance costs

are the interest on borrowings. This line tells you how the company is funded, not how it operates. Two identical factories, one funded by debt and one by equity, show identical operating performance and very different finance costs.
Depreciation and amortisation
spreads the cost of assets bought in earlier years across their useful lives. No cash leaves the company this year, which is the single most important thing to remember about it.
Other expenses

is the catch-all: rent, power and fuel, freight, advertising, travel, professional fees, repairs, insurance. It is usually the line with the most management discretion, and its note is where cost-cutting stories are hiding.

body.title: Which line is it?
body.question: Your company sells a delivery van it no longer needs and books a gain of ₹12 lakh. Where does that gain appear in the P&L?
options: It does not appear in the P&L at all
body.explanation: Selling a fixed asset is not the core business, so the gain sits in other income. This matters when you compare years. A profit boosted by asset sales says nothing about how the business performed.

body.title: What the top line excludes
body.textWithBlank: Revenue from operations is reported net of ___, because that amount is collected on behalf of the government and was never the company's income.
body.explanation: An invoice of ₹118 including 18% GST contributes ₹100 to revenue. The ₹18 is a liability owed to the government until it is paid.

children.text: The Same Waterfall at a Real Company

Here is Britannia Industries, the Kolkata-headquartered biscuits maker listed on NSE and BSE, for the year ended 31 March 2025, on a consolidated basis, using the figures shown on screener.in. Amounts are rounded to the nearest crore, so a subtotal can differ by ₹1 crore.

cells: Operating profit before depreciation and interest

stats.label: Effective tax rate
stats.context: ₹749 crore on ₹2,927 crore of pre-tax profit

children.text: Revenue grew 7.0% while profit grew only 2.1%. That gap is the whole story of the year, and it is invisible if you read only the bottom line. Something between the two lines grew faster than sales. Converting every line into a percentage of revenue, as the third column does, is the fastest way to find it.

body.text: Do not compare a rupee expense across two years and call it control. If revenue grew 7% and freight grew 7%, nothing changed. Always convert to a percentage of revenue first. Finance teams call this common-size analysis, and it takes about five minutes in Excel.

body.title: Revenue up, profit flat
body.scenario: You lead operations at a listed consumer goods company. Revenue is up 7% this year, but profit for the year is up only 2%. In tomorrow's leadership meeting the CEO wants to know where the extra revenue went.
body.prompt: How would you find the answer from the P&L, and what could explain a gap like this?
body.modelAnswer:
How to find it:
1. Put both years side by side and convert every line into a percentage of revenue.
2. Rank the lines by the change in that percentage. The two or three largest movers explain nearly all of the gap.
3. Open the notes behind those lines for the component breakup, then check the MD&A for management's explanation.
What usually explains it:
4. Input costs: wheat, palm oil, packaging or fuel rising faster than selling prices, which shows up in cost of materials.
5. Price versus volume: revenue growing on discounts or mix rather than price, so gross margin falls even as sales rise.
6. Employee cost: increments and new hires landing ahead of the revenue they were meant to generate.
7. Investment spending: a marketing push, a new plant's depreciation starting, or interest on fresh borrowing.
8. One-off items in the base year, such as an asset sale that inflated last year's other income, making this year look weak.
What to present: a bridge from last year's profit to this year's, with each cause quantified, rather than a single explanation.

children.text: The Last Few Lines
Below profit before tax sit four lines that managers rarely need but should recognise.

cells: Large one-off gains or losses, such as a plant closure or a legal settlement
Strip these out before comparing two years
Current tax payable for the year plus deferred tax from timing differences
The effective rate rarely equals the headline corporate tax rate
Gains and losses parked outside profit, such as actuarial changes in gratuity liabilities
Almost never relevant to a manager, but it explains why total comprehensive income differs from profit
Profit attributable to shareholders divided by the weighted average number of shares
The number the stock market reacts to

body.latex: \text{Basic EPS} = \frac{\text{Profit attributable to equity shareholders}}{\text{Weighted average number of equity shares}}
body.caption: Britannia FY25: about ₹2,178 crore across roughly 24.1 crore shares, giving an EPS of about ₹90

body.title: Why the tax line is never a neat 25%

children.text: Britannia's effective tax rate works out to 25.6%, which is close to but not equal to any headline rate. Three things pull it around.
The regime the company chose:
many Indian companies moved to the concessional corporate tax regime, giving an effective rate of about 25.17% including surcharge and cess, in exchange for giving up most incentives.
Deferred tax:
accounting rules and tax rules depreciate assets differently, so the tax charged in the books and the tax actually paid this year diverge. The difference is parked as deferred tax.
Group mix:
in consolidated accounts, subsidiaries in different countries and states are taxed at different rates, so the blended rate lands somewhere in between.
For a manager, the practical rule is simple: use profit before tax when you compare operating performance, because the tax line carries decisions that have nothing to do with how the business ran.

body.description: The P&L table here shows ten years side by side. Try converting three years of lines into percentages of revenue and see which cost line moved most.

body.title: Read one real P&L this week
steps: Open the consolidated P&L of your employer or a listed competitor for the last two years.
Write down revenue from operations and other income separately, and check how much of profit came from outside the core business.
Convert every expense line into a percentage of revenue for both years.
Circle the line whose percentage moved most, and read its note.
Calculate the effective tax rate: tax expense divided by profit before tax.
Write one sentence explaining the change in profit that a manager in another department would understand.

cards.definition: Income from the core business, reported net of GST, discounts and expected returns.
Income from outside the core business: interest, dividends, rent, gains on asset sales.
The cost of raw materials and packaging actually used in production during the period.
An adjustment, not a cost, correcting for production that is still unsold at year end.
Salaries, bonus, provident fund, gratuity, share-based payments and staff welfare.
Interest and related charges on borrowings. A funding cost, not an operating cost.
Large one-off gains or losses that distort year on year comparison.
Restating every P&L line as a percentage of revenue so that years and companies can be compared.

points: The P&L is a waterfall from revenue to profit, and Schedule III fixes the order of the lines for every Indian company.
Revenue from operations is the core business and is net of GST. Other income is everything else, and it is not performance.
Changes in inventories is a correction for unsold production, not a cost.
Finance costs reflect how a company is funded, and depreciation is a non-cash charge for assets bought in earlier years.
Convert every line into a percentage of revenue before comparing years, otherwise growth hides cost problems.
Compare operating performance at the profit before tax level, because exceptional items and tax carry decisions unrelated to operations.

body.text: Kesari Foods is fictional. Britannia Industries figures are FY25 consolidated numbers as shown on screener.in, rounded to the nearest crore and used only to illustrate how a P&L is read. Nothing here is investment advice.
